title: Tu BiShvat
hookLine: the new year for trees, marked with fruits of the land of Israel

lines: AN OLD MAN PLANTS A CAROB.
cards: The Talmud tells of a man named Honi. Walking along a road, he sees an old man planting a carob tree. Honi asks: how long until that tree gives fruit?
Seventy years, says the old man. Honi can't believe it: you think you'll live seventy more years to eat from it? The old man answers, more or less: I found this world full of carob trees.
My grandparents planted them for me. So I'm planting this one for my grandchildren. Honi, the story goes, falls asleep for seventy years.
When he wakes, a young man is picking carobs from that tree.

teach.h: FOUR NEW YEARS, ONE FOR TREES.
teach.b: The Mishnah lists four new years in the Jewish calendar, each with its own purpose; one is for trees.
The House of Shammai said it falls on the first of the month of Shevat; the House of Hillel said the fifteenth, and again, Hillel's view is followed.
In Hebrew, fifteen is written tet vav, which sounds like tu: Tu BiShvat, the fifteenth of Shevat. It began as a date for bookkeeping.
The Torah has rules about fruit trees, how a tree's first years of fruit are left alone, and which year's produce is tithed, so you need a birthday to count a tree's age.

teach.h: THE RAINS HAVE FALLEN, THE SAP RISES.
teach.b: The Talmud explains the date: by the fifteenth, most of the year's rain in the land of Israel has fallen, and the sap is rising. Over time, it became a celebration.

Later, mystics following the Kabbalists of Safed shaped a Tu BiShvat seder: fruits and nuts eaten in a set order, and in one telling, cups of wine that move from white to red, like winter turning to spring.

teach.h: FRUITS OF THE LAND, AND PLANTING.
teach.b: People eat the fruits the Torah praises in the land: "a land of wheat and barley, and vines and fig-trees and pomegranates; a land of olive-trees and honey," a honey the rabbis read as date honey.
In Israel and around the world, it's also a day for planting trees and caring for the earth.

teach.h: FOR IS THE TREE OF THE FIELD MAN?
teach.b: The Torah even forbids cutting fruit trees during a siege, asking: "for is the tree of the field man?" A tree can't run away. It's in your care.

how: On Tu BiShvat, many Jews eat fruits, especially those the Torah links to the land of Israel, some hold a Tu BiShvat seder of fruits and wine, and many plant trees or support planting.

o: the fifteenth of Shevat, a new year for trees
a spring day for planting the year's crops
a day to give names to Israel's trees

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

the Torah's rules about fruit and tithes needed a birthday for trees.
the House of Shammai's date is the one followed
Shammai said the first of Shevat; Hillel said the fifteenth, and Hillel's view is followed.
the Torah forbids cutting fruit trees in a siege

games.q: you're the old man by the road. a stranger laughs: you'll never live to eat from that carob tree. what do you say?
o: you're right, I'll plant something faster.
others planted for me, so I plant for others.
I'll live long enough, you'll see.
games.why: he says he found the world full of carob trees his ancestors planted, and plants for his grandchildren.

practice: Hold a fruit if you have one, or picture one, and think of the tree it came from, the years it took to grow, the rain, the person who picked it; then taste it slowly.
If you say blessings, the Jewish blessing over tree fruit thanks God, who creates the fruit of the tree. Then think of one thing you're planting that you may never see finished.

wordCard.voice: Tu BiShvat. The fifteenth of Shevat: the new year for trees, marked with fruit, planting and thanks.

orig.note: Hebrew: the fifteenth of Shevat; tet (9) plus vav (6) make fifteen.

carryVoice: Your line: a birthday for trees. Happy new year to every one of them. Until next time.
